title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 36
paragraphs: So the men charged with this distasteful work carried out their orders. Meanwhile other master-builders were busy making the bridges, in this way. They laid fifty-oared galleys and triremes together side by side, three hundred and sixty of them to form the bridge on the Black Sea side, and three hundred and fourteen on the other, the vessels lying at an angle to the current of the Hellespont (but crosswise to the Pontus), so as to take the strain of the cables. Having arranged them thus, they dropped very large anchors — those on the Pontus side to hold against the winds blowing out from within, those on the western and Aegean side against the south-east and south winds. They also left an opening as a channel, so that any ship that wished might sail in or out of the Pontus in small vessels. This done, they proceeded to tighten the cables, straining them with wooden windlasses — no longer using the two kinds of rope separately, but assigning to each bridge two ropes of white flax and four of papyrus. The thickness and the quality of workmanship were the same for both; but the flax ropes were heavier in proportion, and of this rope one cubit weighed a talent. With the strait now bridged, they sawed logs into sections equal to the width of the bridge, laid them atop the tensioned cables, and, having set them in order, fastened them together. Once that was done, they carried on brushwood, and having set the brushwood in place, they heaped earth on top of it and tamped it down firmly. Finally they built a barrier along each side, so that the pack animals and horses would not be frightened by looking out over the sea.
